I have farmed these fields in Quzhou County for more than forty years, and I know what this soil can do. I never went to school, but I learned everything from my parents and from watching my neighbors season after season. This year, like most years, I will plant winter wheat on all nine mu of my land when the autumn rains come. After we harvest the wheat in early June, I will immediately put in summer maize — that is the rotation everyone in our village follows, and it is what reliably feeds my family. 

For the wheat, I will buy the improved seeds from the agricultural supply shop, the same kind the other farmers are using. I will rotary till the soil before sowing and spread compound fertilizer as a base dressing, then topdress with urea when the wheat starts to green up in spring. I will irrigate three times — once after sowing if it is dry, once at jointing, and once at heading — and I will spray pesticides four times when I see aphids or rust starting on the leaves. 

For the maize, I will use hybrid seeds, whatever the shop recommends this year, and sow them directly into the wheat stubble without tilling. There is no time to waste between the wheat harvest and the maize sowing, and the soil is already loose enough. I will give it less fertilizer than the wheat, irrigate twice if the summer turns dry, and spray pesticides four times to keep the stem borers away. I expect around five hundred kilograms of wheat per mu and a bit more for the maize, which is about what I usually get.
